questions.q: The diagram shows the repeating unit of an addition polymer. Which monomer was used to make it?

figure.alt: A repeating unit in square brackets with n: two carbon atoms in a row; the first carries two hydrogen atoms, the second a hydrogen atom and a CH3 group; a bond from each end carbon passes out through the brackets.

questions.solution: An addition polymer's repeating unit contains the two carbons that formed the monomer's C=C, now joined by a single bond. Putting the double bond back between the two carbons gives \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCH_{3}}\), propene. Propane has no C=C, so it cannot polymerise.

questions.q: The diagram shows a section of an addition polymer chain. Which monomer was used to make it?

figure.alt: A section of an addition polymer chain: four carbon atoms in a row, each carrying one hydrogen atom above and one CH3 group below.

questions.solution: Every carbon in the chain carries one H and one \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), so the repeating unit is two chain carbons, each with H and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\): \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH{=}CHCH_{3}}\), but-2-ene. (A common slip is to take one chain carbon as the repeating unit; a repeating unit from an alkene always has two chain carbons.) Two repeating units are shown.

options.A: Monomers containing a C=C double bond join together, and the polymer is the only product.
options.B: Monomers join together and a molecule of hydrogen is lost each time.
options.C: A polymer is broken down into its monomers by reaction with water.
options.D: Monomers with two functional groups join together, and a small molecule such as water or HCl is lost for each link formed.

questions.solution: In condensation polymerisation each monomer has two reactive groups (or two monomers have one type each), and every link formed eliminates a small molecule, usually water or hydrogen chloride. Joining C=C monomers with no other product is addition polymerisation; breaking a polymer down with water is hydrolysis.

questions.q: The diagram shows the repeating unit of a polyester. Which two monomers could be used to make it?

figure.alt: A repeating unit in square brackets with n: an O, a C=O, a benzene ring joined at opposite corners, another C=O, an O, then CH2–CH2.

questions.solution: Break each ester link, –C(=O)–O–, and add back OH to the C=O and H to the O. This gives \(\mathrm{HOOC{-}C_{6}H_{4}{-}COOH}\), benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, and \(\mathrm{HOCH_{2}CH_{2}OH}\), ethane-1,2-diol. The polymer is Terylene (PET). Each monomer needs two functional groups; ethanol and benzoic acid have one each.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine, \(\mathrm{H_{2}N(CH_{2})_{6}NH_{2}}\), and hexanedioic acid, \(\mathrm{HOOC(CH_{2})_{4}COOH}\). Which is its repeating unit?
questions.solution: Each amine group loses an H and each acid group loses its OH, forming amide links. The repeating unit is one of each monomer joined, with open bonds at both ends: \(\mathrm{-NH(CH_{2})_{6}NHCO(CH_{2})_{4}CO-}\). The acid has six carbons in total but only four \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) groups. (A common slip is to leave a COOH on the end; a repeating unit has a bond at each end instead.)

questions.q: Kevlar, whose repeating unit is shown, is strong enough to be used in body armour. Which explains its strength?

figure.alt: Repeating unit of Kevlar in square brackets with n: N–H, a benzene ring joined at opposite corners, N–H, C=O, a second benzene ring joined at opposite corners, then C=O.

options.A: Hydrogen bonds form between the N–H groups of one chain and the C=O groups of a neighbouring chain, and the flat, rigid chains line up closely.
options.B: The chains are joined to each other by covalent cross-links between the benzene rings.
options.C: The chains are held together by ionic bonds between the amide groups.
options.D: The chains contain only C–C and C–H bonds, so there are only van der Waals forces between them.

questions.solution: Kevlar is a polyamide. The δ+ hydrogen of N–H on one chain hydrogen bonds to the lone pair of a δ− oxygen of C=O on the next chain. The benzene rings make the chains straight and rigid, so they pack in close, ordered sheets with many hydrogen bonds. There are no covalent cross-links between chains.

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 can be made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioyl dichloride, \(\mathrm{ClOC(CH_{2})_{4}COCl}\), instead of hexanedioic acid. Which small molecule is eliminated as each link forms?
questions.solution: The N–H hydrogen of the amine combines with the Cl of the acyl chloride group, so HCl is eliminated: \(\mathrm{-NH_{2} + ClOC- \rightarrow -NHCO- + HCl}\). Water is eliminated only when the dicarboxylic acid is used. The acyl chloride reacts faster, at room temperature.

questions.q: Poly(lactic acid) is a polyester made from a single monomer, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)COOH}\). Which is its repeating unit?
questions.solution: The OH group of one molecule reacts with the COOH group of the next, losing water and forming an ester link. Each unit keeps one O from its OH group and the C=O of its acid group, so the repeating unit is \(\mathrm{-OCH(CH_{3})CO-}\). (A common slip is to keep both oxygens of the COOH, which counts the ester oxygen twice.) \(\mathrm{-OCH_{2}CH_{2}CO-}\) would come from 3-hydroxypropanoic acid.

questions.q: The repeating unit of Kevlar is \(\mathrm{C_{14}H_{10}N_{2}O_{2}}\). A sample of Kevlar has an average \(M_{\text{r}}\) of 119 000. How many repeating units does an average chain contain? (\(A_{\text{r}}\): H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, O 16.0)
questions.solution: \(M_{\text{r}}\) of the repeating unit \(= 14 \times 12.0 + 10 \times 1.0 + 2 \times 14.0 + 2 \times 16.0 = 238.0\). (A common slip is to count monomer molecules, two per repeating unit, which doubles the answer.) Number of repeating units \(= \frac{119\,000}{238.0} = 500\).

questions.q: Why can polyesters and polyamides be broken down by hydrolysis, while poly(alkenes) cannot?

options.A: Ester and amide links contain a polar C=O group whose δ+ carbon can be attacked by nucleophiles such as water or hydroxide ions; poly(alkenes) have only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds.
options.B: Poly(alkenes) still contain C=C double bonds, which are too strong to break.
options.C: Polyesters and polyamides are ionic, so they dissolve in water.
options.D: Poly(alkenes) have hydrogen bonds between their chains, which stop water reaching them.

questions.solution: Hydrolysis needs a site that a nucleophile can attack. The carbonyl carbon in an ester or amide link is δ+, so water (with acid) or hydroxide ions can attack it and break the link. A poly(alkene) chain is saturated and has no polar bonds, so it is chemically inert and not biodegradable.

questions.q: Terylene (PET) is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. What are the organic products?
questions.solution: Alkaline hydrolysis breaks the ester links, giving the diol and the salt of the dicarboxylic acid: ethane-1,2-diol and sodium benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate, \(\mathrm{NaOOC{-}C_{6}H_{4}{-}COONa}\). (A common slip is to give the free acid: that forms only with acid hydrolysis, or when acid is added afterwards.)

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 is heated under reflux with excess hydrochloric acid. What are the products?
questions.solution: Acid hydrolysis breaks the amide links to give hexanedioic acid and the diamine. The diamine is a base, so in excess acid both amine groups are protonated: the product is the salt \(\mathrm{ClH_{3}N(CH_{2})_{6}NH_{3}Cl}\), hexane-1,6-diammonium chloride. (A common slip is to give the free diamine, which is what alkaline hydrolysis gives, along with the sodium salt of the acid.)

questions.q: Why must the waste gases from incinerating PVC be treated before they are released?

options.A: They contain hydrogen chloride, a toxic, acidic gas, which can be removed by reacting it with a base.
options.B: They contain only carbon dioxide and water, which must be cooled.
options.C: They contain methane, which must be burned off.
options.D: They contain sulfur dioxide from the sulfur atoms in PVC.

questions.solution: PVC, poly(chloroethene), contains chlorine, so burning it releases hydrogen chloride. HCl is toxic and forms acid rain. Gases are passed through a "scrubber" containing a base, such as calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, to neutralise it. PVC contains no sulfur.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of recycling waste polymers?

options.A: It releases toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride into the air.
options.B: It uses more crude oil than making new polymer.
options.C: Waste must be collected and sorted into different types of polymer, which is costly and labour-intensive.
options.D: It takes up large areas of land for hundreds of years.

questions.solution: Different polymers have to be separated before they can be melted and remoulded, and collecting, cleaning and sorting is expensive. The recycled polymer can also be of lower quality. Releasing hydrogen chloride is a problem of incineration, and taking up land for a long time is a problem of landfill.

questions.q: What is meant by using waste polymers as a feedstock?

options.A: Burning them to release energy for generating electricity
options.B: Burying them in landfill so they slowly break down
options.C: Melting them and moulding them into new objects
options.D: Cracking them to produce small molecules that are used to make new chemicals and polymers

questions.solution: A feedstock is a raw material for a chemical process. Waste polymers can be cracked into smaller molecules (such as alkenes) that are then used to make other chemicals or new polymers. Burning them for energy is incineration, and melting and remoulding is mechanical recycling.

questions.q: The polyamide whose repeating unit is shown is made from a single monomer. Which monomer?

figure.alt: A repeating unit in square brackets with n: N–H, then a carbon carrying H and CH3, then C=O.

questions.solution: The repeating unit is –NH–CH(\(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\))–CO–: one nitrogen and a C=O on the same carbon chain, joined through a carbon carrying \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\). Adding H to the N and OH to the C=O gives \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH(CH_{3})COOH}\), 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine). 3-aminopropanoic acid would give –NH–\(\mathrm{CH_{2}CH_{2}}\)–CO–, with no side group.

questions.q: Which linkage joins the repeating units in a polyamide?
questions.solution: A polyamide is held together by amide (peptide) links, \(\mathrm{-CONH-}\), formed between a carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) group and an amine group. \(\mathrm{-COO-}\) is the ester link in a polyester.
